title: Emrys and the Postcard
premise: Eleven years ago, Dominic Kavanagh testified against the family that ran Harborlight's docks, then vanished into a new name, a daughter, and a bookshop with the blinds half-drawn. When a postcard they never sent—dated the week they disappeared—arrives via a dead-letter cache, it draws the attention of Wren Okafor, the festival organizer and investigative journalist whose brother's disappearance is tangled in the same old case. As the autumn festival approaches, Dominic must choose between the safety of small steps and the dangerous truth: that Wren's brother may still be alive, and that the Kavanagh name was never the real secret. The novel ends at the festival's closing night, when Dominic testifies a second time—this time not to survive, but to come home—choosing Wren and the found family of the town over the invisibility that once saved them.
about_author: Ada Vane is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who writes romances about people who rebuild their lives one careful shelf at a time. She lives on a coast much like Harborlight, where the postcards always arrive late and the festivals always end too soon.

chapters.title: Dead Letter, Live Address
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. While sorting a donation bin of undelivered mail, Dominic finds a postcard postmarked eleven years ago—in their own handwriting, to an address they've never admitted living at. The beat is quiet dread: the past has learned their new address.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Steps
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A ordinary day at the bookshop—daughter Ivy's school run, regulars, careful routines—showing the life Dominic built to stay invisible. The beat is tenderness shadowed by vigilance; we see what Dominic stands to lose.

chapters.title: Wren, With a Press Badge
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The new festival organizer sweeps into the bookshop soliciting donations and immediately notices Dominic flinch at the word 'Harborlight.' Wren, chasing a story about her brother's old disappearance, files Dominic away as a lead. The beat is magnetic, uneasy attraction.

chapters.title: What the Postcard Said
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Alone at night, Dominic rereads the postcard: a single line promising 'I'll tell them everything'—signed with a name Dominic buried. Flashback fragments reveal the testimony eleven years ago and the price paid. The beat is guilt resurfacing like a bruise.

chapters.title: Committee of One
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren strong-arms Dominic onto the festival committee to stay close, and the two clash over the program—her ambition against his caution. The beat is sparks disguised as friction; neither admits why the other matters.

chapters.title: Ivy Asks About Before
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Ivy, twelve and sharp, finds the postcard and asks who Emrys was. Dominic lies badly. The beat is parental fear: the lie that protected her now threatens to be the thing that costs her trust.

chapters.title: The Docks at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren walks the derelict docks her brother vanished from, cross-referencing his last letters with the festival archives—and finds Dominic's old name on a witness list that was sealed. The beat is the thrill and danger of getting close to the truth.

chapters.title: Lending Pieces
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A storm traps Dominic and Wren in the shop after hours; over bad wine they trade almost-truths. Dominic offers pieces of the past but withholds the whole. The beat is intimacy as negotiation—closeness without surrender.

chapters.title: Someone Else Remembers
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A man from the old docks family appears in the shop, buys nothing, and leaves a message: 'Some debts keep interest.' The beat is cold fear—the price of survival is coming due, and it has been watching.

chapters.title: The Sealed File
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren pulls strings to see the sealed testimony and learns Dominic's testimony implicated the man her brother worked for. She confronts Dominic, who shuts down. The beat is betrayal on both sides—she used him; he used silence.

chapters.title: Half a Heart on Loan
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In the fallout, Dominic almost runs—the old escape reflex, bags half-packed, Ivy asleep upstairs. Ivy wakes and asks to come along this time. The beat is the moment the escape fantasy breaks against the life Dominic actually loves.

chapters.title: Festival Lights, Festival Lies
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Festival week opens; the town glitters while Wren publishes a teaser column that names no one but points straight at the docks. The old family's lawyer calls her editor. The beat is rising stakes—her story is now a fuse.

chapters.title: The Man Who Kept the Mail
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic tracks the retired postal worker who sat on the dead-letter cache and learns the postcard was mailed the week of the disappearance—by someone trying to give Dominic a way out that never arrived. The beat is grief for the life that might have been.

chapters.title: Emrys, Spoken Aloud
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds Dominic at the tide pools and, instead of pressing, says the buried name gently—offering partnership, not an exposé. Dominic tells her everything: the smuggling, the brother's last sighting, the testimony. The beat is the whole heart, finally risked.

chapters.title: What Happened to Daniel Okafor
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Following Dominic's account, Wren learns her brother didn't drown—he was smuggled out alive and has been hiding under another name, too afraid to return. The beat is vertigo: the answer she chased for a decade is a living man who chose fear.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The old family's patriarch offers Dominic a clean trade: recant the testimony's aftermath publicly, and the past stays buried. He mentions Ivy's school by name. The beat is corruption's quiet voice—safety offered at exactly the wrong price.

chapters.title: Found Family, Assembled
chapters.summary: Ensemble, mostly Dominic's POV. The shop's regulars, Ivy, and Wren throw Dominic an impromptu birthday in the back room—candles, terrible singing, no questions. The beat is belonging: the first time Dominic sees that the town was never a hiding place, it was a home.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's full story is set to run festival morning; her editor kills it under legal pressure, and her press credentials are pulled. She must choose between the story and the town. The beat is the cost of power wielded from the outside.

chapters.title: Closing Night
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. At the festival's closing ceremony, before the whole town and with Wren's hand in theirs, Dominic takes the microphone and tells the truth—about Emrys, the docks, the threats, the offer. The beat is the climax: testimony as an act of love, not survival.

chapters.title: Interest Paid
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The confession forces the district attorney to reopen the case; the patriarch is arrested at the harbor as the fireworks go up. Wren publishes everything, her byline restored. The beat is vindication that feels less like victory than like setting down a heavy bag.

chapters.title: The Letter That Finally Arrived
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Daniel Okafor walks into the bookshop, older, unannounced, and asks if the town would have him back. Ivy shelves a book between them like a bridge. The beat is forgiveness extended to a stranger who is also a mirror.

chapters.title: Postmarked Home
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, closing with Wren's. One year later: the expanded shop, Ivy's essay about her parent's courage, a postcard on the counter—this one sent and delivered on time, addressed to both of them. The beat is resolution: survival was the price; love is the dividend.
